newsitem.title: USA: Inflation steady, sales rose in September - reports.
newsitem.headline: Inflation steady, sales rose in September - reports.

text.p: Wholesale prices advanced modestly in September and retail sales recorded healthy gains, the government said Friday, offering still more proof that inflation remains under control despite a growing economy.

The Labour Department said the Producer Price Index rose 0.2 percent last month compared to August's 0.3 percent increase. Sales at retail stores posted a surprisingly strong 0.7 rise, the Commerce Department said in a separate report.

"This really is a good positive indicator that inflation isn't taking off, said Bill Cheney, chief economist at John Hancock Financial Services. "To have a good month for retail sales at the same time is really the best of both worlds."
An unexpectedly robust showing by the automobile industry had a notable impact on both reports.

September's surge in business for new-car dealers helped push total retail sales to a seasonally adjusted $205.7 billion. The figures, which exceeded Wall Street forecasts, followed a revised 0.2 percent decline in August sales.

During September, dealer sales of new cars rose 1.7 percent after a revised 0.5 percent August increase, the Commerce Department said. Excluding autos, September retail sales were up a more modest 0.4 percent.

In the Labour Department's produce price report, moderate increases in food and energy prices helped to restrain wholesale inflation. Excluding often-volatile food and energy prices, the "core rate" of inflation moved up 0.3 percent due in part to higher prices for passenger cars and light trucks.

Passenger car prices jumped 1.2 percent in September, registering the biggest one-month gain since November 1993, when prices rose 1.3 percent. Light truck prices soared 1.3 percent last month. Without the impact of those gains, the PPI would have risen only 0.1 percent, the Labour Department said.
The report confirmed that inflation remained relatively tame at the wholesale level and cheered financial markets, pushing stocks higher and long-term interest rates lower.
The Dow Jones industrial average rose 43.98 points to 5,965.65 in afternoon trading.

In the inflation-sensitive bond market, the bellwether 30-year Treasury rose about half a point, pushing its yield, which moves in the opposite direction, to 6.85 percent from 6.89 percent late on Thursday.
Economists surveyed by Reuters had forecast a rise of 0.3 percent in the PPI, with a gain of 0.2 percent in the core rate.
Economists have become increasingly concerned that rising labour costs in a tightening job market could lead to a pickup in inflation in the months ahead.

But inflation data so far have suggested businesses are reluctant to pass along higher labour costs in the form of price increases. Labour costs, however, have a far bigger impact on the Consumer Price Index, which is due next Wednesday, than on the Producer Price Index.

The PPI measures prices that wholesalers pay for goods and materials from suppliers. The CPI includes prices for goods as well as services, and service industries account for the bulk of the nation's jobs.

"Wages rather than materials and goods will be the primary driver for this blip up in inflation later this year," said Raymond Worseck, chief economist at A.G. Edwards & Sons. "One of these months we're going to get a surprise that will spook the bond market when these wage increases start to come in."

Friday's PPI showed that food prices rose 0.2 percent in September, compared with a jump of 1.0 percent a month before. Energy prices gained 0.2 percent, after rising 0.7 percent in August. The increase was paced by a 0.9 percent jump in gasoline and a gain of 2.0 percent in heating oil prices.
In the retail sales report, the government said sales at general merchandise stores rose 0.3 percent and sales at clothing stores fell 0.1 percent.
Total August sales had been reported rising 0.2 percent but that was sharply revised to a show a 0.2 percent decline.

Sales of durable goods such as cars and other long-lasting items rose 0.9 percent in September after a 0.1 percent decline in August. Sales of non-durables such as food and clothing grew 0.6 percent after falling 0.3 percent in August.

Also on Friday, the University of Michigan's consumer sentiment survey, released only to paying subscribers, showed consumer confidence remaining at high levels. The preliminary reading for October rose to 94.8 from 94.7 in September's final reading.
